'''Primetals Technologies Limited''' is an engineering and plant construction company headquartered in London, United Kingdom, with numerous locations worldwide. It serves clients in the metals industry, both the ferrous and the nonferrous metals sector.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://steelguru.com/steel/Primetals%20Technologies%20to%20supply%20automation%20technology%20to%20the%20rolling%20mills%20of%20Ulsan%20Aluminum%20in%20Korea/527387?type=steel|title=Primetals Technologies to supply automation technology to the rolling mills of Ulsan Aluminum in Korea|last=steelguru|website=SteelGuru India|language=en|access-date=2018-12-07|archive-date=2018-12-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181209124331/https://steelguru.com/steel/Primetals%20Technologies%20to%20supply%20automation%20technology%20to%20the%20rolling%20mills%20of%20Ulsan%20Aluminum%20in%20Korea/527387?type=steel|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://worcester.ma/2018/01/inbox-jan-20-27-news-and-notes-from-wcac-st-peter-marian-primetals-worcester-roots-project-more/|title=Inbox [Jan. 20-27]: News and notes from WCAC, St. Peter-Marian, Primetals, Worcester Roots Project + more|last=Staff|first=Sun|website=worcester.ma|date=20 January 2018 |language=en-US|access-date=2018-12-07|archive-date=2018-12-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20181209124356/https://worcester.ma/2018/01/inbox-jan-20-27-news-and-notes-from-wcac-st-peter-marian-primetals-worcester-roots-project-more/|url-status=live}}</ref>  It was established as a [[joint venture]] between [[Siemens|Siemens VAI]] Metals Technologies and [[Mitsubishi Heavy Industries|Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery]] in 2015. As of 2020, Primetals Technologies is a joint venture of [[Mitsubishi Heavy Industries]] and partners.

== Overview ==

=== Operations ===
Primetals Technologies operates as a full liner, i.e., a comprehensive supplier for the metals industry. Their portfolio covers all aspects of the iron and steel production process and includes several nonferrous metals technologies, as well as comprehensive metallurgical services. These processes include but are not limited to [[beneficiation]], [[Direct reduced iron|direct reduction]], [[Basic oxygen steelmaking|oxygen steelmaking]], [[Electric arc furnace|electric steelmaking]], [[continuous casting]], [[Rolling (metalworking)|hot and cold rolling]], and [[Pickling (metal)|processing]]. They are also active in the digitalization of various aspects of the metals industry, including improvements in [[automation]] technologies, services, increasing the use of [[Artificial intelligence in industry|artificial intelligence]], and increasing the use of [[robotics]] to improve the safety of iron and steel works.

==== Green Steel at Primetals Technologies ====
As of May 2022, the formation of a new global task force titled "Green Steel" was announced to combine the competencies in the metals industry with cross-industrial competencies of the larger [[Mitsubishi Heavy Industries|Mitsubishi Heavy Industries Group]].<ref>{{Cite web |last=Westin |first=Björn |date=18 May 2022 |title=Primetals Technologies Launches New Task Force to Lead Transition to Green Steel |url=https://www.primetals.com/press-media/news/primetals-technologies-launches-new-task-force-to-lead-transition-to-green-steel |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=Primetals Technologies |language=en-US}}</ref> Recognizing the severity of the global [[Climate change|climate crisis]], the steel industry at large has been recognized as a major contributor of [[Greenhouse gas emissions|carbon emissions]] into the atmosphere producing eight percent of global [[Carbon dioxide|CO<sub>2</sub>]] emissions in 2020.<ref>{{Cite web |last1=Hoffmann |first1=Christian |last2=Van Hoey |first2=Michel |last3=Zeumer |first3=Benedikt |date=3 June 2020 |title=Decarbonization challenge for steel |url=https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/metals-and-mining/our-insights/decarbonization-challenge-for-steel |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=www.mckinsey.com}}</ref> With several environmental technologies in their portfolio, Primetals Technologies is at work to help reduce the carbon footprint of the metals industry.

== History ==
=== Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery ===
{{prose|section|date=September 2019}}

In May 2000, [[Mitsubishi Heavy Industries]] and [[Hitachi]] announced the establishment of a broad-based partnership in metals rolling mills.<ref>{{Cite web |title=HITACHI : News Releases : May 30, 2000 |url=https://www.hitachi.com/New/cnews/E/2000/0530/000530B.html |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=www.hitachi.com}}</ref> In October 2000, a joint venture company, MHI-Hitachi Metals Machinery, Inc. was established to handle sales and related engineering activities of metal rolling mills and downstream facilities.<ref>{{Cite web |title=HITACHI GLOBAL : News Releases from Headquarters : September 27, 2000 |url=https://www.hitachi.com/New/cnews/E/2000/0927/ |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=www.hitachi.com}}</ref> In 2002, the name was changed to Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery, Inc.<ref>{{Cite web |title=HITACHI : Investors |url=https://www.hitachi.com/IR-e/ir/pis.html |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=www.hitachi.com}}</ref>
In 2004, Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery, Inc. U.S.A. was established.

* 2006 – Acquisition of New Gencoat, Inc., U.S.A
* 2006 – MHMM receives contract for supply of pickling line-tandem cold mill from [[Shougang Jingtang]] Inc., China
* 2007 – Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery, Inc., China established
* 2010 – Start-up of endless billet-welding and rolling mill at [[POSCO]], South Korea
* 2010 – Founding of Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery South Asia Private Ltd. 
* 2012 – Start-up of No. 2 Hot-Rolling Mill at Usiminas Cubatão, Brazil
* 2013 – Integration of IHI Metaltech rolling mill business<ref>{{Cite web |last=Corporation |first=I. H. I. |title=IHI Metaltech and Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery Reach Basic Agreement On Integration of Rolling Mill Businesses｜Industrial Systems and General-purpose Machinery｜2013FY｜News｜IHI Corporation |url=http://www.ihi.co.jp/all_news/2013/industrial_general_machine/2013-6-13 |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=株式会社IHI |language=en}}</ref>
* 2013 – Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery acquires shares in Concast Ltd., India<ref>{{Cite web |date=2013-05-23 |title=Japan's Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals acquires shares in Concast India |url=https://www.fastmarkets.com/insights/japans-mitsubishi-hitachi-metals-acquires-shares-in-concast-india |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=Fastmarkets |language=en}}</ref>
* 2013 – Acquisition of majority shares of Hasegawa Gear Works, Ltd.<ref>{{Cite web |date=January 9, 2014 |title=Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery Acquires Full Stake in Manufacturer of Gear Reducers |url=https://www.aist.org/news/steel-news/2014/january/mitsubishi-hitachi-metals-machinery-acquires-full |access-date=November 4, 2022 |website=www.aist.org}}</ref>

=== Siemens VAI Metals Technologies ===
====1938–1955====
VAI, whose parent company was VA Technologie AG,<ref name="VAI"/> began as the plant building operation of [[Voestalpine|Vereinigte Österreichische Eisen und Stahlwerke]] (VÖEST) but became a separate operation in 1946.<ref name="Steel">{{cite news |date=September 1997 |title=VAI - Plantmaking Specialists |volume=21 |page=15 |work=Steel Times International |issue=5}}</ref> In 1938, the American company H.A. Brassert & Co. began the designs for the Reichswerke in Linz before withdrawing in 1939.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Aylen |first1=Jonathan |title=Stalinism, autarchy, espionage and Marshall Aid: How US strip mill technology came to Europe |journal=The International Journal for the History of Engineering & Technology |date=2 January 2019 |volume=89 |issue=1–2 |pages=92–121 |doi=10.1080/17581206.2020.1782618 |s2cid=221115131 }}</ref>

At the end of WWII, Austria was occupied by the allied forces, and due to the air raids during the war, all industrial assets were severely damaged.<ref name=":0">{{Cite journal |last=Cappel |first=Jürgen |date=26 May 2022 |title=70 Years of LD-Steelmaking—Quo Vadis? |url=https://mdpi-res.com/metals/metals-12-00912/article_deploy/metals-12-00912-v4.pdf?version=1654309104 |journal=Metals |volume=12 |issue=912|page=912 |doi=10.3390/met12060912 |doi-access=free }}</ref> In July 1945, the "Alpine Montan AG Hermann Göring" plant was renamed to "Vereinigte Österreichische Eisen- und Stahlwerke" ([[Voestalpine|VÖEST]]<ref name="va1938">{{cite web|url=https://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/overview/history/1938-1945.html|title=1938-1945 - voestalpine|publisher=- voestalpine.com|access-date=2012-12-05|archive-date=2012-07-30|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120730112458/http://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/history/1938-1945.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="va1945">{{cite web|url=https://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/overview/history/1945-1955.html|title=1945-1955 - voestalpine |publisher=voestalpine.com|access-date=2012-12-05|archive-date=2012-11-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121112195201/http://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/history/1945-1955.html|url-status=live}}</ref>) (United Austrian Iron and Steel Plants) and separated from the Alpine Mountain AG.<ref name="va1945"/> The plant was returned to the newly founded Republic of Austria in July 1946 as part of what would become the ÖIAG (Austrian Industries AG).<ref name="va1945"/><ref name=":1">{{Cite book |last=Cliff |first=Pratten |title=International Directory of Company Histories |work=voestalpine AG |publisher=St. James Press |year=2010 |editor-last=Derek Jacques |editor-first=Paula Kepos |volume=115 |pages=473–478}}</ref> For the plant's reconstruction, Voestalpine used funding from the Marshall Plan.<ref name=":0" /> In 1947 the first blast furnace, a [[Open hearth furnace|Siemens-Martin]] open hearth furnace, and first coke ovens started production.<ref name=":1" />  In 1948, with the launch of the “Iron and Steel Plan,” which allocated the production of flat steel to Linz and the production of long products to Donawitz.<ref name=":0" /> This included the production of finished products in a heavy-plate mill and the construction of a new slab and hot-strip mill in Linz.<ref name=":0" />

However, with production based on the open-hearth furnace, the future of flat production in Linz would be too expensive.<ref name=":0" /> Therefore, a new manufacturing process, i.e., what would become the [[Basic oxygen steelmaking|Linz-Donawitz-process]], began development in 1949 and the patent was applied for in 1950.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Werk Donawitz Entwicklung und Umfeld 50 Jahre LD-Verfahren |publisher=Voestalpine Bahnsystem GmbH |year=2002 |location=Munich, Germany}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Schober |first=Michaela C. |title=The story of the Linz-Donawitz process |publisher=voestalpine AG |year=2013 |location=St. Pölten, Austria}}</ref> After construction, two LD-Converters were commissioned, one in 1952<ref name="VAI2001" /> in Linz, and the other in 1953 in Donawitz.

====1956–1973====
Voest-Alpine Industrieanlagenbau began as a division of [[Voestalpine|VÖEST]] in 1956.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.primetals.com/en/pressandmedia/archive-metals-magazine/Documents/002_Metals-Magazine_1_2007_I_and_%20S_Conference.pdf|title=The Steel World Meets in Linz|last1=Böhm|first1=Christian|last2=Gould|first2=Lawrence|work=[[Metals & Mining]]|date=2007-02-01|access-date=2017-08-10|archive-date=2017-08-11|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170811011351/https://www.primetals.com/en/pressandmedia/archive-metals-magazine/Documents/002_Metals-Magazine_1_2007_I_and_%20S_Conference.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite magazine |id={{ProQuest|1368077896}} |title=VAI - Plantmaking specialists |magazine=Steel Times International |location=Redhill |volume=21 |issue=5 |date=September 1997 |page=15 }}</ref>

With the invention of the LD-process and experiences gained from the complete reconstruction after the war, VÖEST, partnered with the [[Krupp|Fried. Krupp]] company in Essen, Germany, began the construction of the first LD steelmaking plant outside Austria in Rourkela, India, in 1958.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/history/1956-1962.html|title=1956-1962 VÖEST up to the Beginning of the Formation of the Group|publisher=voestalpine.com|access-date=2017-08-11|archive-date=2017-08-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170812055736/http://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/history/1956-1962.html|url-status=live}}</ref>  In 1960, the management of [[:de:Wiener Brückenbau und Eisenkonstruktions A. G.|Wiener Brückenbau und Eisenkonstruktions AG]] (WBB), later renamed Voest-Alpine Hebetechnik- und Brückenbau AG, is transferred to VÖEST.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web |title=Historie - voestalpine |url=https://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/overview/history/ |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=www.voestalpine.com |language=en}}</ref> VÖEST continued to expand worldwide and expanded their network of customers to amount to 274 business relationships in 87 countries by 1968.<ref name=":2" /> In 1973, the two nationalized iron and steel industries VÖEST and Österreichisch-Alpine Montangesellschaft (Alpine) merged and became [[voestalpine|Vöest-Alpine AG]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/history/1974-1985.html|title=1974-1985 VOEST-ALPINE AG up to the Reform of ÖIAG|publisher=voestalpine.com|access-date=2017-08-11|archive-date=2017-08-12|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170812055546/http://www.voestalpine.com/group/en/group/history/1974-1985.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

====1974–1994====
When the [[1973 oil crisis|oil crisis]] started in 1973, the metallurgical industry was severely affected in all parts of the world (see also, "[[steel crisis]]"). In Austria, this coincided with the creation of Vöest-Alpine AG and between 1974 and 1976 several other companies joined the group, including Gebrüder Böhler & Co AG, Schoeller-Bleckmann Stahlwerke AG, and Steirische Gußstahlwerke AG, making up the "Vereinigte Edelstahlwerke AG (VEW).<ref name=":2" /> While the merger of these companies strengthened the position of Vöest-Alpine AG, the impact of the steel crisis led the company to refocus its efforts. In 1977, the group was divided into four divisions: steelworks, processing, finished goods, and industrial plant engineering.<ref name=":2" /> In 1978, industrial plant engineering was also under the direct control of the management board.<ref name=":2" />

In the late 1970s, VOEST-ALPINE AG, as VAI, began developing the "COREX process" with Korf Engineering GmbH, originally known as the "KR method."<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zhou |first1=Xiao Lei |last2=Shi |first2=Zhe |last3=Zhang |first3=Gui Fang |last4=Du |first4=Zhong Ning |date=October 2014 |title=Comparison of COREX and COSRI Process Technology Development |url=https://www.scientific.net/AMM.678.612 |journal=Applied Mechanics and Materials |volume=678 |pages=612–615 |doi=10.4028/www.scientific.net/AMM.678.612 |s2cid=110251557 |issn=1662-7482|url-access=subscription |doi-access=free }}</ref> In 1985 the crisis came to a head, and VOEST-ALPINE declared bankruptcy.<ref name=":2" /> In fall of 1986, the "Concept for a New VOEST-ALPINE" was introduced along with the establishment of the [[Österreichische Beteiligungs AG|Österreichische Industrieholding Aktiengesellschaft (ÖIAG)]].<ref name=":2" />

Finally, in 1988, the Austrian government decided to partially privatize the ÖIAG, forming Voest-Alpine Stahl AG (VA Stahl), while placing Voest-Alpine Industrieanlagenbau (VAI, also VAI-BAU) under Maschinen- und Anlagenbauholding AG.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Hinterhuber |first1=Hans |url=https://wug.akwien.at/WUG_Archiv/1988_14_4/1988_14_4_0475.pdf |title=Wirschaft und Gesellschaft - WuG |last2=Obernosterer |first2=Karl |last3=Unterweger |first3=Andreas |work=ÖIAG und IRI - zwei Unternehmen auf dem Weg zu einer neuen Identität |publisher=Kammer für Arbeiter und Angestellte für Wien, Abteilung Wirschaftswissenschaft und Statistik |year=1988 |volume=14 |location=Vienna |pages=475–504}}</ref>

====1995–2014====
In 1993, after a restructuring of the ÖIAG group, [[:de:VA Technologie|VA Technologie AG (VA Tech)]] emerged and became the parent company to VAI.<ref>{{Cite web |date=2015-01-15 |title=Die Geschichte der ÖIAG « WirtschaftsBlatt.at |url=http://wirtschaftsblatt.at/home/nachrichten/oesterreich/1286883/Die-Geschichte-der-OIAG |access-date=2022-11-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150115105053/http://wirtschaftsblatt.at/home/nachrichten/oesterreich/1286883/Die-Geschichte-der-OIAG |archive-date=15 January 2015 }}</ref><ref name=":3">{{Cite web |title=VA Technologie AG, VA Tech |url=https://austria-forum.org/af/AEIOU/VA_Technologie_AG%2C_VA_Tech |access-date=2022-11-25 |website=Austria-Forum |language=de}}</ref> By 1995, VAI operated in 45 countries and had 2000 engineers, with revenue of $841 million.<ref name=Welch>{{cite news|title=Voest plans deal with Fuchs|last=Welch|first=David T.|work=[[American Metal Market]]|date=3 March 1995|volume=103|issue=42|page=8|issn=0002-9998}}</ref>

In 1995, VAI bought its first shares of Fuchs Systems Inc. (Fuchs Systemtechnik GmbH), a German-based manufacturer of [[electric arc furnace]]s  and other equipment for manufacturing steel, with plants in [[Mexico]] and [[Salisbury, North Carolina]].<ref name="Welch" /><ref name="pitzer1">{{cite news |last=Pitzer |first=Sara |date=1999-09-24 |title=Fuchs plans to lay off 59 workers |work=[[Salisbury Post]] |url=http://www.salisburypost.com/september99/092499c.htm |url-status=live |access-date=2010-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080719000339/http://www.salisburypost.com/september99/092499c.htm |archive-date=2008-07-19}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |date=2001-05-10 |title=VA Technologie AG acquires Fuchs Systemtechnik GmbH from Siemens AG |url=http://www.alacrastore.com/storecontent/Thomson_M&A/VA_Technologie_AG_acquires_Fuchs_Systemtechnik_GmbH_from_Siemens_AG-1182112040 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230315120441/http://www.alacrastore.com/storecontent/Thomson_M&A/VA_Technologie_AG_acquires_Fuchs_Systemtechnik_GmbH_from_Siemens_AG-1182112040 |url-status=dead |archive-date=15 March 2023 |access-date=2010-05-19 |publisher=Thomson Financial Mergers & Acquisitions}}</ref> The Salisbury plant had 230 employees in 1997.<ref name="Atotech">{{cite news |last=Elkins |first=Ken |date=2001-05-21 |title=$5M expansion proposed for Atotech's headquarters |work=[[Charlotte Business Journal]] |url=http://charlotte.bizjournals.com/charlotte/stories/2001/05/14/newscolumn5.html?page=2 |url-status=live |access-date=2010-05-18 |archive-url=https://archive.today/20120712031727/http://charlotte.bizjournals.com/charlotte/stories/2001/05/14/newscolumn5.html?page=2 |archive-date=2012-07-12}}</ref>

As of 1997, ÖIAG owned 24% and Voest-Alpine Stahl owned 19.05% of the stock in VAI's parent VATech.<ref name="Steel" /><ref name=":3" /><ref name="Kvaerner">{{cite news |date=1999-06-10 |title=Voest Alpine acquires Kvaerner business |work=[[Pittsburgh Business Times]] |url=http://pittsburgh.bizjournals.com/pittsburgh/stories/1999/06/07/daily13.html |url-status=live |access-date=2010-06-29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220423100233/https://www.bizjournals.com/pittsburgh/stories/1999/06/07/daily13.html |archive-date=2022-04-23}}</ref> In September 1999, VAI completed its acquisition of the [[Norway|Norwegian]]-owned [[Kværner|Kvaerner A.S.A.]] metals equipment group, including operations in [[France]], [[Spain]], [[Italy]], [[Germany]], [[China]], [[India]] and [[Great Britain]].<ref name="southpointe">{{cite news |last=Elliott |first=Suzanne |date=1999-11-19 |title=Voest-Alpine to relocate 300 to Southpointe |work=[[Pittsburgh Business Times]] |url=http://pittsburgh.bizjournals.com/pittsburgh/stories/1999/11/22/story1.html |url-status=live |access-date=2010-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220423100224/https://www.bizjournals.com/pittsburgh/stories/1999/11/22/story1.html |archive-date=2022-04-23}}</ref> VAI subsidiary Voest-Alpine Industries Inc.<ref>{{cite news |date=2004-01-21 |title=Dateline: Pittsburgh |work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/04021/263691-28.stm |url-status=dead |access-date=2010-09-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220423100231/https://old.post-gazette.com/pg/04021/263691-28.stm |archive-date=2022-04-23}}</ref> had its American headquarters in [[Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania]].<ref name="Kvaerner" /> In 1999, Voest-Alpine Industries, part of VA Tech North America, moved all its Pittsburgh operations to [[Southpointe (Cecil, Pennsylvania)|Southpointe]] in [[Washington County, Pennsylvania|Washington County]]. At the time, the company had just taken over [[Kværner|Kværner A.S.A.'s]] metals equipment group. Voest-Alpine Industries also operated in [[Eastlake, Ohio]], and [[Benton Harbor, Michigan]].<ref name="southpointe" /><ref>{{cite news |last=Fitzpatrick |first=Dan |date=2000-04-09 |title=Views differ on the prospects for commercial real estate |work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]] |url=http://www.postgazette.com/businessnews/20000409comreal.asp |url-status=live |access-date=2010-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060519010123/http://www.postgazette.com/businessnews/20000409comreal.asp |archive-date=2006-05-19}}</ref> The metals automation division of Voest-Alpine Industries relocated from Eastlake to Southpointe in 2002.<ref>{{cite news |date=2002-05-23 |title=Voest-Alpine combining Ohio, Southpointe offices |work=[[Pittsburgh Business Times]] |url=http://pittsburgh.bizjournals.com/pittsburgh/stories/2002/05/20/daily40.html |url-status=live |access-date=2010-06-08 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20040920141454/http://pittsburgh.bizjournals.com/pittsburgh/stories/2002/05/20/daily40.html |archive-date=2004-09-20}}</ref>

As of 1999, Voest-Alpine Industries owned 49 percent of Fuchs. Although the company laid off 59 employees in Salisbury, Fuchs was "the market leader", and the parent companies intended to keep Fuchs in business.<ref name="pitzer1" /> The layoffs resulted from an [[1997 Asian financial crisis|economic crisis]] in [[Asia]], as well as lower demand for American steel resulting from the low import prices. However, the Asian market was returning by 1999, and [[Europe]] and [[South America]] were also possible new markets.<ref>{{cite news |last=Pitzer |first=Sara |date=1999-11-21 |title=Expert says manufacturing jobs were on the way out even without trade agreement |work=Salisbury Post |url=http://www.salisburypost.com/november99/112199a.htm |url-status=live |access-date=2010-05-18 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080513045957/http://www.salisburypost.com/november99/112199a.htm |archive-date=2008-05-13}}</ref> In 2001, Voest-Alpine Industrieanlagenbau bought the rest of Fuchs Systems, which became VAI Fuchs and added VAI Technometal.<ref name="VAI2001" /> In May 2001, however, Fuchs closed the Salisbury plant, its only American facility, because half the customers were [[Chapter 11, Title 11, United States Code|bankrupt]] or close to it.<ref name="Atotech" /> AlloyWorks bought three of the buildings, and the fourth became a medical office.<ref>{{cite news |last=Elkins |first=Ken |date=2001-11-26 |title=Amtrak link to Statesville could be off track |work=[[Charlotte Business Journal]] |url=http://www.bizjournals.com/charlotte/stories/2001/11/26/newscolumn6.html |url-status=live |access-date=2012-12-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160131194123/http://www.bizjournals.com/charlotte/stories/2001/11/26/newscolumn6.html |archive-date=2016-01-31}}</ref> Also, in 2001, the steel industry worldwide experienced a downturn due to lower prices, though [[continuous casting]] (for which VAI was the world's top company) continued its positive results, especially in [[China]]. VAI reduced its six business areas to four: Iron & Steelmaking (the largest); Rolling & Processing; Automation, and Metallurgical Services.<ref name="VAI2001" />

Also in 2001, VAI's continuous casting operation added a casting and [[Rolling (metalworking)|rolling]] mill for ultra-wide medium thickness slabs for [[IPSCO Steel]] in [[Mobile, Alabama]],<ref name=VAI2001>{{cite journal|title=VAI — creativity in technology|journal=Steel Times International|date=July–August 2002|page=44}}</ref> with what were believed to be the world's largest one-piece cast mill housings at 350 tons.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.allbusiness.com/manufacturing/primary-metal-mfg-iron-steel/6479082-1.html|title=IPSCO Steel (Alabama) Construction Proceeds on Schedule; World's Largest Mill Stands Set inPlace|work=Business Wire|date=2000-05-08|access-date=2010-05-20}}</ref> The automation business completed a quality control project along with Voest-Alpine Stahl.<ref name=VAI2001/>

In 2003, VAI subsidiary Voest-Alpine Services & Technologies Corp. became majority owner of Steel Related Technology of [[Blytheville, Arkansas]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.post-gazette.com/pg/03267/225276-28.stm|title=Dateline: Pittsburgh|last=Hill|first=Natalie|work=[[Pittsburgh Post-Gazette]]|date=2003-09-24|access-date=2010-09-02|archive-date=2022-04-23|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220423100206/https://old.post-gazette.com/pg/03267/225276-28.stm|url-status=dead}}</ref>

After the [[Siemens]] purchase of VA Technologie AG completed in July 2005, VAI became Siemens VAI, a part of the Siemens Industrial Solutions and Services Group.<ref name=VAI>{{cite web|url=http://www.allbusiness.com/primary-metal-manufacturing/iron-steel-mills-ferroalloy/237953-1.html|title=VAI's continuous casting and rolling conference|last=Smith|first=Tim|publisher=allbusiness.com|date=2004-09-01|access-date=2010-08-04|archive-date=2008-12-08|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081208090041/http://www.allbusiness.com/primary-metal-manufacturing/iron-steel-mills-ferroalloy/237953-1.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.azom.com/News.asp?NewsID=3506|title=EU Commission Approves Siemens' Acquisition of VA Tech|publisher=AZoM|date=2005-07-14|access-date=2010-05-25|archive-date=2008-09-19|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20080919123742/http://www.azom.com/News.asp?NewsID=3506|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|title=Siemens Consolidates Voest After Takeover; SMS Objects|journal=Metal Producing & Processing|date=July–August 2005|page=11}}</ref> Siemens VAI was later named Siemens VAI Metals Technologies GmbH & Co.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/private/snapshot.asp?privcapId=5479002|title=Siemens VAI Metals Technologies GmbH & Co.: Company Overview|publisher=businessweek.com|access-date=2010-05-19|archive-date=2012-10-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121007044533/http://investing.businessweek.com/research/stocks/private/snapshot.asp?privcapId=5479002|url-status=dead}}</ref> and also referred to as VAI Group, which was created from VAI and Siemens electrical engineering and automation businesses.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.automation.com/content/siemens-announces-systems-for-strip-cooling-in-hot-rolling-mills|title=Siemens announces systems for Strip Cooling in Hot Rolling Mills|work=automation.com|date=2007-05-18|access-date=2010-06-02|archive-date=2011-07-28|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728101540/http://www.automation.com/content/siemens-announces-systems-for-strip-cooling-in-hot-rolling-mills|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://hbia.org/m_associates_vai.cfm|title=Siemens VAI Metals Technologies GmbH & Co.|publisher=The Hot Briquetted Iron Association|access-date=2010-06-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110522051124/http://www.hbia.org/m_associates_vai.cfm|archive-date=2011-05-22|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.prdomain.com/companies/S/Siemens/newsreleases/200631829934.htm|title=Siemens VAI supplies equipment for new metal-coating line at Steelscape, USA|publisher=PRdomain.com|date=2006-03-17|access-date=2010-06-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110616193146/http://www.prdomain.com/companies/S/Siemens/newsreleases/200631829934.htm|archive-date=2011-06-16|url-status=usurped}}</ref> Siemens Group Industrial Solutions and Services also included Voest-Alpine Services and Technologies (VAST). Both Siemens units operated from the Pittsburgh area.<ref name=VAST>{{cite web|url=http://info.industry.siemens.com/press/Details.aspx?pressArticleId=895&languageId=2|title=Siemens Continues Caster Maintenance Services at Mittal Steel, Sparrows Point/USA|publisher=Siemens Industry News and Press|date=2006-08-10|access-date=2010-06-09|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716065148/http://info.industry.siemens.com/press/Details.aspx?pressArticleId=895&languageId=2|archive-date=2011-07-16|url-status=dead}}</ref> VAST provided mill maintenance services to steel and aluminum manufacturers from eleven locations: [[Baltimore, Maryland]]; [[North East, Maryland]]; [[New London, Ohio]]; [[Milan, Ohio]]; [[Benton Harbor, Michigan]]; [[Bethel Park, Pennsylvania]]; [[Blytheville, Arkansas]]; [[Charleston, South Carolina]]; [[Decatur, Alabama]]; and [[Erie, Pennsylvania]], in the United States and [[Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario]], in [[Canada]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.prdomain.com/companies/S/Siemens/newsreleases/200681234843.htm|title=Siemens continues caster maintenance services at Mittal Steel, Sparrows Point/USA|publisher=PRdomain.com|date=2006-08-10|access-date=2010-06-29|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110616193151/http://www.prdomain.com/companies/S/Siemens/newsreleases/200681234843.htm|archive-date=2011-06-16|url-status=usurped}}</ref>

===Primetals Technologies===

==== 2014 - Present ====

|url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170716043311/http://primetals.com/en/about-us/company-profile |archive-date=2017-07-16 |access-date=2017-07-26 |publisher=Primetals Technologies}}</ref> in which equity ownership shares were 51% for Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery and 49% for Siemens AG.<ref>{{cite news |date=2014-06-03 |title=02/06/14 – Mitsubishi purchases majority stake in Siemens VAI |publisher=[[International Iron Metallics Association]] |url=http://metallics.org.uk/mitsubishi-purchases-majority-stake-in-siemens-vai-02062014/ |url-status=live |access-date=2014-08-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804013025/http://metallics.org.uk/mitsubishi-purchases-majority-stake-in-siemens-vai-02062014/ |archive-date=2017-08-04}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |last=Gillingwater |first=Paul |date=2014-05-07 |title=Mitsubishi acquires metal producer Siemens VAI |work=[[The Local]] |url=https://www.thelocal.at/20140507/japans-mitsubishi-siemens-vai-takeover |url-status=live |access-date=2017-08-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804012848/https://www.thelocal.at/20140507/japans-mitsubishi-siemens-vai-takeover |archive-date=2017-08-04}}</ref>  The joint venture, Primetals Technologies Limited, started operations in January 2015.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Kinkartz |first1=Sabine |last2=Mazumdaru |first2=Srinivas |date=2014-05-07 |title=Siemens set for a major revamp |work=[[Deutsche Welle]] |url=http://www.dw.com/en/siemens-set-for-a-major-revamp/a-17618367 |url-status=live |access-date=2017-08-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170804020926/http://www.dw.com/en/siemens-set-for-a-major-revamp/a-17618367 |archive-date=2017-08-04}}</ref> In 2019, Primetals Technologies together with Mitsubishi Heavy Industries acquired ABP Induction Systems.<ref name=fp170719>{{cite news|url=https://www.foundry-planet.com/equipment/detail-view/mhi-and-primetals-technologies-to-acquire-abp-induction-systems/|title=MHI and Primetals Technology to acquire ABP Induction Systems|work=Foundry Planet|date=2019-07-17|access-date=2019-09-24|archive-date=2019-09-24|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190924151041/https://www.foundry-planet.com/equipment/detail-view/mhi-and-primetals-technologies-to-acquire-abp-induction-systems/|url-status=live}}</ref>

On September 30, 2019, Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and Siemens AG reached the agreement that MHI will acquire Siemens’ 49 percent stake in Primetals Technologies. The transaction was completed at the end of January 2020.<ref>{{cite news |date=2019-10-01 |title=10/01/19 – Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery to acquire Siemens' stake in Primetals Technologies |publisher=[[Mitsubishi Heavy Industries]] |url=https://www.mhi.com/news/story/191001.html |url-status=live |access-date=2019-10-11 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191012005757/https://www.mhi.com/news/story/191001.html |archive-date=2019-10-12}}</ref>

In Spring 2021, the international private equity investor [[:de:Mutares|Mutares]] completed the acquisition of Primetals Technologies France from Primetals Technologies, Ltd., subsequently changing the name to Clecim France.

In Fall 2021, Primetals Technologies, Ltd. transferred its shares of Primetals Technologies Italy to Callista Private Equity, a financial investment company located in Munich, Germany.<ref>{{Cite web |date=12 November 2021 |title=Primetals Technologies Italy Sold to German Investor Callista Private Equity |url=https://www.primetals.com/press-media/news/primetals-technologies-italy-sold-to-german-investor-callista-private-equity |access-date=2022-11-04 |website=Primetals Technologies |language=en-US}}</ref>

extract: Primetals Technologies Limited is an engineering and plant construction company headquartered in London, United Kingdom, with numerous locations worldwide. It serves clients in the metals industry, both the ferrous and the nonferrous metals sector.  It was established as a joint venture between Siemens VAI Metals Technologies and Mitsubishi-Hitachi Metals Machinery in 2015. As of 2020, Primetals Technologies is a joint venture of Mitsubishi Heavy Industries and partners.
